edges.source_hint: Wikipedia 'Cell theory' (history section; per the order's supplied quote, 'In 1855, Rudolf Virchow added the third tenet to cell theory'); Encyclopedia Britannica 'Rudolf Virchow'.
edges.note: Honest gap: the same source states the pre-existing-cells idea 'had already been proposed by Robert Remak; it has been suggested that Virchow plagiarized Remak.' Remak has no corpus node, so his contribution cannot be represented by a competing founder edge. Positioned as a standard founder edge with this priority question recorded here rather than as `disputed`, mirroring how this corpus already records the Lavoisier/conservation-of-mass Jean Rey and Lomonosov priority questions as supported + note rather than disputed -- but this is a judgment call for QC to confirm against live sources, not a settled one.
edges.rationale: Virchow is credited with adding the third, constitutive tenet of the modern doctrine (cells arise only from pre-existing cells, 'omnis cellula e cellula'), completing the theory as it is taught today -- a direct contribution to the concept's own content, not a downstream application, so founded_or_formalized fits better than the runner-up `influenced`, which would understate a credited addition to the theory's core claims. The Schwann/Schleiden founder edges already promoted in this corpus explicitly flagged Virchow's absence as an honest gap; this edge closes it.
edges.uncertainty: I have not live-verified the Remak plagiarism allegation's weight or mainstream standing this session -- if QC's live check finds a substantial, sourced, live scholarly camp crediting Remak over Virchow (rather than a single flagged allegation), this should be reweighed toward clause-6 v2's asymmetric-disputed branch instead of supported + note. Separately, 'adding a tenet' to an already-founded theory is a different grain of contribution than Schwann/Schleiden's original 1830s work, and whether founded_or_formalized is the precisely correct relation (versus a lesser one) is itself a judgment call.

edges.source_hint: Wikipedia 'Germ theory of disease' (history section; per the order's supplied quote, 'Basic forms of germ theory were proposed by Girolamo Fracastoro in 1546, and expanded upon by Marcus von Plenciz in 1762'); Encyclopedia Britannica 'Girolamo Fracastoro'.
edges.note: Marcus von Plenciz (the 1762 'expander') has no corpus node and gets no edge, the same way Playfair (uniformitarianism's refiner) never received one. This mirrors the corpus's existing James-Hutton-not-Charles-Lyell disposition for uniformitarianism: origin credit to the named proposer of the theory's basic form, not to a later expander/systematizer.
edges.rationale: The source's own history places the theory's origin with Fracastoro in 1546 (two centuries before the 19th-century experimental confirmation), which is the exact reasoning the prior wave's QC used to decline both Pasteur and Koch as founders of this same concept ('the theory is stated to originate with Fracastoro'). It is also the same origin-vs-later-contributor pattern already used in this corpus to promote Hutton over Lyell for uniformitarianism.
edges.uncertainty: 'Basic forms... proposed' is a hedge in the source's own wording, softer than an unqualified founding claim. I have not live-verified the full article text, and I do not know whether structural identity data for this concept independently corroborates Fracastoro the way it corroborates Pasteur (per the prior wave's decision report) -- if a live check finds Fracastoro absent from that signal while Pasteur is present, QC should weigh that tension explicitly rather than let this proposal resolve it. There is also an unaddressed historical question of how cleanly Fracastoro's contagion theory (De Contagione, 1546) is distinguished from contemporaneous miasma theory, which a live check should confirm.

edges.source_hint: Wikipedia 'Entropy' (history section; per the order's supplied quote calling Clausius the 'originator of the concept of entropy' and describing his 1865 definition as 'the quotient of an infinitesimal amount of heat to the instantaneous temperature'); Encyclopedia Britannica 'entropy' and 'Rudolf Clausius'.
edges.rationale: Clausius coined the term 'entropy' and gave it its first precise mathematical definition (dS = dQ/T) in 1865, an origination claim stated without hedging in the source -- founded_or_formalized fits cleanly since this is squarely originating the specific named concept the node represents, unlike Boltzmann's later reframing of the same pre-existing quantity (proposed separately below with a different relation).
edges.uncertainty: This concerns specifically the naming and mathematical definition of entropy; it does not address the broader, more distributed history of the second law of thermodynamics itself (Carnot's 1824 cycle work, and William Thomson/Lord Kelvin's parallel 1850s statement of the second law), handled as a separate, non-competing claim on the disciplinary founder edge to subfield:thermodynamics proposed below. I have not live-verified the exact 1865 quotation this session.

edges.source_hint: Encyclopedia Britannica 'Rudolf Clausius' and 'thermodynamics'; general history-of-physics/thermodynamics textbooks' treatment of Clausius's 1850 paper on the mechanical theory of heat and his mathematical statement of the second law.
edges.note: Honest gap: Sadi Carnot (1824 cycle work, the underlying physical insight) and William Thomson/Lord Kelvin (parallel 1850s statement of the second law) are standardly credited alongside Clausius in this history; neither is a corpus node, so this edge cannot be balanced by a co-founder edge this batch. Not a claim that Clausius worked alone.
edges.rationale: Beyond entropy specifically, Clausius gave thermodynamics its first rigorous mathematical statement of the second law (1850, restated 1854/1865), standardly treated as foundational to thermodynamics as a mathematical science. subfield:thermodynamics currently carries no founder-class edge from any person, a real coverage gap. Proposed under the order's invitation to add a disciplinary founder claim on the same terms as the concept-level edge -- a distinct, separately sourced grain, mirroring the corpus's existing pattern of parallel subfield- and concept-level founder edges (e.g. Schwann/Schleiden to both cell-biology and cell-theory).
edges.uncertainty: Thermodynamics' foundational history is more distributed than cell theory's (see the Carnot/Kelvin gap noted above), so 'founder of the subfield' is a broader and more contestable grain than 'originator of the entropy concept'. I have not live-verified sourcing for this specific disciplinary-level framing this session.

edges.source_hint: Wikipedia 'Entropy' (history section; per the order's supplied quote: Boltzmann in 1877 'visualized a probabilistic way to measure the entropy of an ensemble of ideal gas particles, in which he defined entropy as proportional to the natural logarithm of the number of microstates such a gas could occupy'); a Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Boltzmann's work in statistical physics, if one exists under that or a similar title -- unconfirmed this session.
edges.rationale: Boltzmann did not originate the concept of entropy -- Clausius had already named and mathematically defined it twelve years earlier (this batch's sibling edge) -- he supplied a new formal, statistical-mechanical framing (entropy proportional to the log of the number of microstates) for the pre-existing quantity. This matches `formalizes` ('a formal mathematical/logical framing for something that already existed') precisely rather than `founded_or_formalized`, per the order's own definitional guidance distinguishing the two relations for exactly this Clausius/Boltzmann pair.
edges.uncertainty: As far as I can tell from this corpus, this would be the first `formalizes` edge sourced from a `person` node rather than a `subfield`/`field` -- every existing formalizes edge (29 of them) runs discipline-to-discipline. The taxonomy definition does not restrict `formalizes` to non-person sources and the order's own phrasing tracks this reading closely, but QC should treat the relation choice itself (formalizes vs. founded_or_formalized, whose own definition includes 'helped ... formalize') as the primary judgment call to check. I have not live-verified the exact 1877 quotation or confirmed the named Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry actually exists under that title this session.

edges.source_hint: Encyclopedia Britannica 'Ludwig Boltzmann'; general history-of-physics textbooks' treatment of the kinetic theory of gases, the Boltzmann equation, and the H-theorem as founding statistical mechanics.
edges.note: Honest gap: James Clerk Maxwell (earlier 1860s kinetic-theory and velocity-distribution work) and Josiah Willard Gibbs (later, 1902, systematic formalization) are standardly credited alongside Boltzmann as founders of statistical mechanics; neither is a corpus node, so this edge cannot be balanced by a co-founder edge this batch. Not a claim that Boltzmann worked alone.
edges.rationale: Boltzmann's kinetic-theory and statistical-mechanical work (the Boltzmann equation, the H-theorem, and the statistical entropy formula proposed as a separate edge above) is standardly credited as founding statistical mechanics as a rigorous subfield of physics. subfield:statistical-physics currently carries no founder-class edge from any person, a coverage gap this closes, proposed on the same disciplinary-founder basis invited for Clausius.
edges.uncertainty: See the Maxwell/Gibbs honest gap above -- a live check may find the mainstream framing gives Maxwell equal or greater originating credit for the kinetic theory specifically, with Boltzmann's distinctive contribution being the statistical/probabilistic reinterpretation. I have not live-verified sourcing for this specific disciplinary-level framing this session.

edges.source_hint: Encyclopedia Britannica 'Albert Einstein' and 'relativity'; general history-of-physics references on the 1905 special-relativity paper and the 1915 general-relativity field equations.
edges.note: Clause-6 v2 candidate, not resolved here: a live, sourced minority historiographical position (the Einstein-Lorentz-Poincare priority literature, e.g. treatments tracing special relativity's mathematical content substantially to Lorentz's and Poincare's pre-1905/1906 work) contests how much of the credit for special relativity specifically belongs to Einstein alone. General relativity (1915) has no comparable rival claimant. See the companion Poincare edge below, written on `influenced` specifically so it does not contradict this edge regardless of how that dispute is weighed.
edges.rationale: Einstein is the mainstream-credited originator of both special relativity (1905) and general relativity (1915, entirely his own work, with no comparable co-claimant). The concept-wave3-v1 rejection of this concept node named Einstein specifically as the correct founder attribution and declined the node only because he did not yet exist as a person node in this corpus -- this edge closes that gap.
edges.uncertainty: I have not live-verified the current weight or mainstream standing of the Einstein/Poincare/Lorentz priority literature this session. QC should run the Lane B pipeline (live sources, adversarial check) and decide between 'supported + note' (if the dissent reads as a priority/scope qualification, per the Lavoisier/Jean Rey precedent already in this corpus) and 'disputed: true, asymmetric' (if the dissent is substantial and live-sourced enough to meet the clause-6 v2 bar) -- this proposal's confidence and lack of a disputed recommendation should not be read as that determination having already been made.

edges.source_hint: Encyclopedia Britannica 'Henri Poincare' and 'relativity'; general history-of-physics references on Poincare's 1905/1906 papers on the dynamics of the electron and his statement of a relativity principle.
edges.rationale: Poincare's work on the electrodynamics of moving bodies, his articulation of a relativity principle, and his mathematical treatment of the Lorentz transformation are well-documented, substantial contemporaneous/precursor contributions to the surrounding development of relativistic physics. `influenced` (not `founded_or_formalized`) is used deliberately: it records Poincare's real, sourced contribution without asserting a founder-level claim, so this edge does not contradict the Einstein founder edge above regardless of how the priority question is ultimately weighed by QC -- this is how the order's 'handle it under clause-6 v2 rather than by picking a winner' instruction is executed at the edge-choice level, not by attaching a disputed flag to either edge myself.
edges.uncertainty: Confidence held at a moderate level because even `influenced` risks reading as more central than most mainstream treatments credit Poincare with; the boundary between 'influenced the surrounding development' and 'independently arrived at overlapping results' is itself part of the same contested literature flagged on the Einstein edge. This edge is a near-verbatim carry-forward of a draft written for the same candidate in the previously declined concept-wave3-v1 batch (that batch's generator used the same relation and a similar confidence before the node itself was rejected for an unrelated reason -- lack of an Einstein node); I have not re-verified it against new sources this session.
